name: Serial dilution
seoTitle: Serial dilution Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Serial dilution: work out percentage error from number of dilutions and the final solution concentration. A free chemistry calculator with the formula,…
summary: percentage error is what the Serial dilution calculator works out, and it gets there from number of dilutions, the final solution concentration, the volume per use and the pipette error. It is built for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Serial dilution calculator work?
sections.html:
The Serial dilution calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports percentage error in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the method and the error type); then you type in number of dilutions, the final solution concentration, the volume per use and the pipette error.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Serial dilution calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Percentage error=-100 + 100 × minimum volume required ÷ (volume per use × number of uses per dilution)
Dilution factor=(minimum volume required + volume to be moved at each step) ÷ volume to be moved at each step
Dilution factor=(dilutant needed at each step + volume to be moved at each step) ÷ volume to be moved at each step
Starting volume needed=dilutant needed at each step + volume to be moved at each step
Total amount of dilutant needed=dilutant needed at each step × number of dilutions + volume of dilutant to be added
Second solution=(dilution factor)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Method set to Dilution factor, Volume per use = 10 cm³, Number of uses per dilution = 10 and Error type set to Percentage. Working through the relationship above gives Pipette error = -9 cm³ and Starting volume needed = 10 cm³.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Pipette error = -9 cm³ and Starting volume needed = 10 cm³ should be roughly the size you expected from Method set to Dilution factor and Volume per use = 10 cm³.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Serial dilution calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — number of dilutions, the final solution concentration and the volume per use — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Serial dilution calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns percentage error, derived from number of dilutions, the final solution concentration and the volume per use. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Serial dilution calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of dilutions, the final solution concentration, the volume per use and the pipette error, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter starting solution concentration in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Starting solution concentration opens in molars and the chip beside it offers 9 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Pipette error = -9 cm³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Serial dilution calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
